Not only is it good for joining panels, you will find many other uses. Often socks knit on the flatbed knitting machine are seamed using this method. <br><br><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/>It's a neat, attractive, strong seam, that SAVES TIME!<BR><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><br>Follow the video as you are practicing. Use light color yarn (and contrasting colors if possible) so you can see the formation of the sew-as-you-go stitches.<br><br><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><b>Swatch 1:</b><br><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/>Knit a small swatch or use the edge of a previously knit swatch for this sample.<br><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><b>Swatch 2:</b><br><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><ul><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><Li>Cast on a new swatch</li><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><li>On the side opposite the carriage pick up and hang the cast on edge stitch of Swatch 1. Be sure to have the Private/wrong side of Swatch 1 facing you. (purl side facing on both pieces)</li><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><li>Be sure to hang the stitch from swatch one ON THE SAME NEEDLE as the end needle of Swatch 2.  Don't increase, double up the stitches as you join to create the seam.</li><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><li>To reduce bulk,  pick up a single strand (one leg) of the edge stitch</li><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><li>Knit across and back (carriage is on the opposite side of the seam)</li><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><li>Continue picking up stitches from Swatch 1 as you knit Swatch 2</li><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/></ul><br><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><b>TIP:</B><br><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/>Placing yarn markers at regular intervals can be helpful in seaming with any method. For example, as you are knitting the first piece place a yarn marker along the edges every 10, 20 or 25 rows (whatever interval you will remember).<br><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/>As you knit the second piece and sew-as-you-go, the markers will help you match the rows of both pieces perfectly.<char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/></div><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><div class="col-md-4 col-xs-12"><img class="img-thumbnail" src="http://www.knititnow.com/challenge/images/not_enough_needles/sew_You_go2.png"></div><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/></string></var></struct></data></wddxPacket>

details: <wddxPacket version='1.0'><header/><data><struct ><var name='CHALLENGE_ASSIGNID'><string>89</string></var><var name='TYPEOF'><string>HTML</string></var><var name='HTMLCONTENT'><string><strong>You are making progress!</strong> ... we've spent a lot of time planning, practicing and thinking about knitting ... are you ready to do some "real knitting"?<br><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><br><strong>DON'T SKIP THIS SECTION!</strong> <br><br>Your success with this course AND your success with your knitting machine depends on your understanding and mastering the art of knitting gauge swatches.<br><br><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/>Without a swatch we are knitting in the dark.<char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><ul><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><li>How is the final sweater going to feel in the yarn and stitch pattern you've chosen?</li><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><li>Do you have enough yarn?</li><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><li>Do you have enough needles on your machine for the size you chose?</li><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/></ul><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><div class="row"><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><div class="col-md-6 col-lg-5 col-xs-12 col-md-offset-1 text-center"><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><p style="text-align: center;"><strong>SWATCHING IS NOT OPTIONAL</strong></p><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><img class="img-thumbnail" src="//www.knititnow.com/images/blog_images/2017/swatching_is_not_optional.jpg" /></div><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/></div></string></var><var name='FIELDNAMES'><string>CHALLENGE_ASSIGNID,TYPEOF,HTMLCONTENT</string></var></struct></data></wddxPacket>

Knit a marker row (change colors, work a few eyelets across the row or knit a sewing thread in with the main yarn)</li><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><li>Keep knitting sections, marking the tension dial number in each section.  Knit the last section as loosely as possiblle, even if you think this will be too loose ... I'm often very pleasantly surprised at the result.</li><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><li>Transfer every other needle to out of work postion and knit a section - put all needles back into work.</li><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><li>Work a simple tuck, or slip, or any stitch pattern of your choice ... base your tension dial setting on the stockinette sections you just knit.</li><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/></ol><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><blockquote class="smallblock">The point of this exercise is to put the yarn through it's paces ... ignite your creativity, and get a feel for what the yarn can do.  If you don't have a huge cone, you can always re-wind this knitting. BlockTitle: Step 1: Your Success Depends on this Lesson
details: <wddxPacket version='1.0'><header/><data><struct ><var name='CHALLENGE_ASSIGNID'><string>129</string></var><var name='CHALLENGE_COMPONENTID'><string>370</string></var><var name='FIELDNAMES'><string>CHALLENGE_ASSIGNID,CHALLENGE_COMPONENTID,HTMLCONTENT</string></var><var name='HTMLCONTENT'><string><strong>You are making progress!</strong> ... we've spent a lot of time planning, practicing and thinking about knitting ... are you ready to do some "real knitting"?<br><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><br><strong>DON'T SKIP THIS SECTION!</strong> <br><br>Your success with this course AND your success with your knitting machine depends on your understanding and mastering the art of knitting gauge swatches.<br><br><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/>Without a swatch we are knitting in the dark.<char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><ul><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><li>How is the final sweater going to feel in the yarn and stitch pattern you've chosen?</li><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><li>Do you have enough yarn?</li><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><li>Do you have enough needles on your machine for the size you chose?</li><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/></ul><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><div class="row"><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><div class="col-md-6 col-lg-5 col-xs-12 col-md-offset-1 text-center"><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><p style="text-align: center;"><strong>SWATCHING IS NOT OPTIONAL</strong></p><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><img class="img-thumbnail" src="//www.knititnow.com/images/blog_images/2017/swatching_is_not_optional.jpg" /></div><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/></div></string></var></struct></data></wddxPacket>

BlockTitle: Step 2: Gauge swatch verses Tension Swatch
details: <wddxPacket version='1.0'><header/><data><struct ><var name='CHALLENGE_COMPONENTID'><string>309</string></var><var name='CHALLENGE_ASSIGNID'><string>130</string></var><var name='FIELDNAMES'><string>CHALLENGE_ASSIGNID,CHALLENGE_COMPONENTID,HTMLCONTENT</string></var><var name='HTMLCONTENT'><string><div class="row cleanwell"><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><div class="col-md-7"><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><h4><strong>GAUGE SWATCH</strong></h4><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/>The <strong>gauge swatch</strong> is the "official" swatch used when designing a garment.<char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><br><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/>It is knit at a specific size, marked for accurate stitch and row measurement and "dressed" as the final garment will be treated.<br><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><blockquote class="smallblock"><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><em>TIP: Whatever method you use to create a swatch, the key is to correctly measure it and calculate your gauge.</em></blockquote></div><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><div class="col-md-5"><img class="img-responsive" src="//www.knititnow.com/challenge/images/swatch_measure.jpg" /></div><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/></div></string></var></struct></data></wddxPacket>

BlockTitle: Step 2: Gauge swatch verses Tension Swatch
details: <wddxPacket version='1.0'><header/><data><struct ><var name='FIELDNAMES'><string>CHALLENGE_ASSIGNID,CHALLENGE_COMPONENTID,HTMLCONTENT</string></var><var name='CHALLENGE_ASSIGNID'><string>130</string></var><var name='CHALLENGE_COMPONENTID'><string>313</string></var><var name='HTMLCONTENT'><string><div class="row cleanwell"><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><div class="col-md-12 col-xs-12"><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><h4><strong>TENSION SWATCH</strong></h4><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><em>When I pick up a new cone of yarn, I can't wait to thread up my machine and see what the yarn looks like.   From the initial cast on, I start guessing what setting on my tension dial I need to use.  I knit a few inches and reach down and start to feel the resulting fabric. <br /><br />Once I get a feel for the yarn (what machine, general tension setting at stockinette, etc) I create a<strong> tension swatch</strong>.  This helps me fine-tune the tension needed to achieve the fabric I like and allows me to play with various techniques.  <strong>I'm often very surprised that a yarn looks great in tuck, and awful in slip</strong>, for example.  Adding a few eyelets here and there tells me if the yarn will work up in lace.</em><br /> <br /> Let's practice knitting a <strong>tension swatch.</strong></div><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/></div></string></var></struct></data></wddxPacket>

details: <wddxPacket version='1.0'><header/><data><struct ><var name='FIELDNAMES'><string>CHALLENGE_ASSIGNID,CHALLENGE_COMPONENTID,HTMLCONTENT</string></var><var name='CHALLENGE_ASSIGNID'><string>130</string></var><var name='HTMLCONTENT'><string><div class="row well"><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><div class="col-xs-12 col-md-10"><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><ol class="instruction-list"><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><li>Play!</li><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><li>Start knitting stockenette at the tightest tension that will knit.  (If the tension is too tight, you'll see stitches that don't form properly.</li><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><li>Knit 2-4 inches. Knit a marker row (change colors, work a few eyelets across the row or knit a sewing thread in with the main yarn)</li><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><li>Keep knitting sections, marking the tension dial number in each section.  Knit the last section as loosely as possiblle, even if you think this will be too loose ... I'm often very pleasantly surprised at the result.</li><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><li>Transfer every other needle to out of work postion and knit a section - put all needles back into work.</li><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><li>Work a simple tuck, or slip, or any stitch pattern of your choice ... base your tension dial setting on the stockinette sections you just knit.</li><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/></ol><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><blockquote class="smallblock">The point of this exercise is to put the yarn through it's paces ... ignite your creativity, and get a feel for what the yarn can do.  If you don't have a huge cone, you can always re-wind this knitting. At this point, you probably know exactly what you want to do with this yarn.  Knit your Gauge Swatch, dress it and and you are ready to design and knit your sweater.</blockquote><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/></div><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><div class="col-xs-12 col-md-2"><img class="img-responsive" src="http://www.knititnow.com/challenge/images/tension_swatch.jpg" /></div><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/></div><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/></string></var><var name='CHALLENGE_COMPONENTID'><string>311</string></var></struct></data></wddxPacket>

details: <wddxPacket version='1.0'><header/><data><struct ><var name='HTMLCONTENT'><string>To work this type of short row shaping on both sides for your armholes (or sleeves), remember that that shaping is worked OPPOSITE the carriage each time.<br><br><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/>Our previous example:<br><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/>At armhole edge, decrease 3 stitches every other row 2 times, decrease 1 stitch every other row 5 times<br><br><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/>Carriage is set to hold and positioned on the RIGHT<br><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/>RC:000 <ul><li>Pull 3 needles on the left (opposite the carriage) into hold position</li><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><li> Knit to the LEFT</li><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/></ul><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/>RC:001<char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><ul><li>Wrap the first held needle</li><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><li>Pull 3 needles on the right into hold position (opposite the carriage)</li><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><li>Knit from LEFT to RIGHT</li></ul><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/>RC:002<ul><li>Wrap the first held needle of the group nearest the carriage</li><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><li>Pull 3 needles on the left into hold position</li><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><li>Knit RIGHT to LEFT</li></ul><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/>Continue following your pattern, working the shaping on both sides OPPOSITE the carriage.<char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/></string></var><var name='FIELDNAMES'><string>CHALLENGE_ASSIGNID,CHALLENGE_COMPONENTID,HTMLCONTENT</string></var><var name='CHALLENGE_COMPONENTID'><string>1535</string></var><var name='CHALLENGE_ASSIGNID'><string>504</string></var></struct></data></wddxPacket>

Perhaps it’s the gauge and the and the electronics.  Maybe you LOVE your punchcard machine.<br><br><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/>No matter the reason, mastering ONE  machine will go a long way towards knitting sweaters that fit.<br><br><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/>Why?  If you aren’t burdened with figuring out which buttons to push, you’ll be able to focus on techniques that will add to your satisfaction with your finished item.<br><br><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><p style="padding-left: 30px;"><span style="font-weight: 400; color: #9B2764;"><b>Best advice … put all but one machine away for a while and focus on your favorite.</b></span></p><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><div class="well"><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><h3><strong><span style="color: #9B2764;"><i class="fa fa-lightbulb-o fa-2x" aria-hidden="true"></i> Use the same yarn for a while</span></strong></h3><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/>If you are a sewist, you probably wouldn’t use the same sewing pattern with denim and with a knit. Each has its own properties.<br><br><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/>The same for yarn.  Take a natural fiber. Knit 2 swatches.  Let one rest and wet block the other.  When you measure for gauge, you’ll get very different numbers.  If your swatches have any man-made fiber content, hit one with steam and compare …. Lots of variables, with one yarn.<br><br><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/>Switch to a different yarn and do the same thing.  The differences may be even greater.<br><br><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/>The point is, each yarn has its own characteristics.  <span style="color: #9B2764;">Once you learn the “personality” of a particular yarn, stick with it.</span> I know a professional designer who only uses one yarn.  She knits hundreds of custom designer garments.<br><br>When she knits a sleeve, she KNOWS what size it is going to be.  This also allows her to get creative.  She can play with color, she can make colorblock pieces … plus she KNOWS that the sweater is going to fit!</span></p><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/></div></string></var><var name='FIELDNAMES'><string>CHALLENGE_ASSIGNID,CHALLENGE_COMPONENTID,HTMLCONTENT</string></var></struct></data></wddxPacket>

Perhaps it’s the gauge and the and the electronics.  Maybe you LOVE your punchcard machine.<br><br><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/>No matter the reason, mastering ONE  machine will go a long way towards knitting sweaters that fit.<br><br><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/>Why?  If you aren’t burdened with figuring out which buttons to push, you’ll be able to focus on techniques that will add to your satisfaction with your finished item.<br><br><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><p style="padding-left: 30px;"><span style="font-weight: 400; color: #9B2764;"><b>Best advice … put all but one machine away for a while and focus on your favorite.</b></span></p><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><div class="well"><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><h3><strong><span style="color: #9B2764;"><i class="fa fa-lightbulb-o fa-2x" aria-hidden="true"></i> Use the same yarn for a while</span></strong></h3><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/>If you are a sewist, you probably wouldn’t use the same sewing pattern with denim and with a knit. Each has its own properties.<br><br><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/>The same for yarn.  Take a natural fiber. Knit 2 swatches.  Let one rest and wet block the other.  When you measure for gauge, you’ll get very different numbers.  If your swatches have any man-made fiber content, hit one with steam and compare …. Lots of variables, with one yarn.<br><br><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/>Switch to a different yarn and do the same thing.  The differences may be even greater.<br><br><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/>The point is, each yarn has its own characteristics.  <span style="color: #9B2764;">Once you learn the “personality” of a particular yarn, stick with it.</span> I know a professional designer who only uses one yarn.  She knits hundreds of custom designer garments.<br><br>When she knits a sleeve, she KNOWS what size it is going to be.  This also allows her to get creative.  She can play with color, she can make colorblock pieces … plus she KNOWS that the sweater is going to fit!</span></p><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/></div></string></var><var name='FIELDNAMES'><string>CHALLENGE_ASSIGNID,CHALLENGE_COMPONENTID,HTMLCONTENT</string></var></struct></data></wddxPacket>

details: <wddxPacket version='1.0'><header/><data><struct ><var name='CHALLENGE_COMPONENTID'><string>2140</string></var><var name='CHALLENGE_ASSIGNID'><string>763</string></var><var name='HTMLCONTENT'><string>Knit it Now Dynamic patterns are a perfect example of the issue of choosing a size by your body measurements.<br><br><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><div class="row"><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><div class="col-md-8 col-xs-12"></div><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><div class="col-md-4 col-xs-12"><a href="http://www.knititnow.com/knit/sizing.cfm"><img class="img-responsive" src="http://www.knititnow.com/images/sizing/xxs_XXL.jpg"></a></div><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/></div><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><blockquote smallblock"><strong>Sizing and Ease: (we are all different)</strong><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><ul><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/> <char code='09'/><li>Some like it hot (no ease)</li><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/> <char code='09'/><li>Some like it cold (roomy)</li><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/> <char code='09'/><li>Some like it just right (It's your choice!)</li><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/></ul><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/></blockquote><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/>When choosing a size to knit with any knitting pattern, <strong>choose based on the finished garment size</strong>.<br><br><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/>With Knit it Now Dynamic patterns, on the build page of the pattern (where you enter your gauge and select the size) is an interactive chart that shows the finished garment size.  Measure a sweater that you like to determine how much ease you want in your sweater. Chose your size based on the finished size.<br><br><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/>Examine the image below. The measurements on the sizing charts are <strong>body measurements.  BUT the finished size of the garment includes ease.</strong><br><br><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/>It's confusing ... do you agree?<br><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><h3>Body size + Ease = Finished Garment Size</h3><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><a href="http://kin.knititnow.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/03/select_sizing.gif"><img class="aligncenter size-full wp-image-1987" src="http://kin.knititnow.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/03/select_sizing.gif" alt="" width="776" height="436" /></a><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/></string></var><var name='FIELDNAMES'><string>CHALLENGE_ASSIGNID,CHALLENGE_COMPONENTID,HTMLCONTENT</string></var></struct></data></wddxPacket>

(DUH)<char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/>On my standard machine, I've dutifully cast on 60 stitches and knit 60 rows between marked rows .  I marked off 40 stitches and got out my regular ruler, measured and did the math.<char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><em>Being a total non-math person, I can't tell you how many times I've messed up the calculation of my gauge ... even when using a calculator.</em><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><br><br><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/> <char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><div class="row"><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><div class="col-md-2 col-xs-12" align="center"><img class="img-responsive" src="/challenge/images/v2/25/lightbulb_guy_100.jpg" alt="" width="50" /></div><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><div class="col-md-10 col-xs-12"><img class="img-responsive" src=""><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><br><br><br><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><strong>THE EPIPHANY:</strong> I was hand knitting a HK pattern.  Hand knitting the complicated sections of the pattern was fun, but I decided that knitting a whole lot of stockinette (the boring stuff by hand) was dumb.  So I threaded up my machine and started to knit a swatch.<char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/></div><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/></div><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><br><br><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><b>The gauge I needed to match was 24 sts and 30 rows per 4".</b><br><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><ul class="li_7px"><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/> <char code='09'/><li> I cast 60 stitches (so I could easily measure 24 stitches)</li><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/> <char code='09'/><li> I knit a few rows with my main yarn (marking with eyelets the tension gauge)</li><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/> <char code='09'/><li> 2 rows of a contrasting color</li><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/> <char code='09'/><li> Knit 30 rows</li><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/> <char code='09'/><li> 2 rows of a contrasting color</li><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/> <char code='09'/><li> A few main yarn rows and bound off</li><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/> <char code='09'/><li>AT THE SAME TIME I also marked  the stitches that were framing my desired 24 stitches.</li><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/></ul><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><blockquote class="blockquote_style"><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><strong>In other words, instead of marking the traditional number of stitches and rows, I broke the "rules" and marked my DESIRED GAUGE  of 24 stitches and 30 rows as I knit the swatch.</strong></blockquote><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/>I let the swatch rest, then wet blocked it and let it sit overnight.<char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/>The next day, I put my handy-dandy 4" measuring tool down on my swatch.  (see below about my DIY 4" tool)<char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/>As you can see, by the first photo, my stitch gauge was good, but my row gauge needed to be adjusted.  It was easy to see through my tool that I had too many rows to 4".   I adjusted my mast tension, knit another swatch and VOILA!  I was able to match my gauge EXACTLY --- with NO MATH!<br><br><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/> <div class="row"><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><div class="col-12-xs width="300" height="288" /><br> <strong>24 sts x 30 rows = 4" ! Success!</strong></div><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/></div><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><hr class"style13"><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/> <char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><h3>Template</h3><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><div align="center"><img class="img-responsive" src="/challenge/images/v2/25/swatch_template.png" alt="" width="342" height="342" /></div><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/>For my tool, I cut a 4" x 4" square of quilters template plastic (readily available at craft stores) to create my Handy-dandy tool. details: <wddxPacket version='1.0'><header/><data><struct ><var name='HTMLCONTENT'><string><center><img class="img-responsive" src="/challenge/images/v2/82/ellens_funnel_gif.gif"></center><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><br><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><i class="fa fa-lightbulb-o fa-2x" aria-hidden="true"></i> Designer Ellen Kindsvater ran with the idea of a simple Funnel neck pullover. Here are her designer elements to the basic design.<br>A few minor changes to Big Hug, knit on the standard gauge machine with a textured stitch pattern and WOW!  A completely different look from the same pattern.<br><br><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><ul><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><Li>G-Carriage Stitch pattern (see below)</li><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><Li>She simplified the shape sleeve for less shaping with the g-carriage</li><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><Li>3/4" funnel for less bulk</li><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><Li>No ribbing</li><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><Li>Back is 2" longer than the front</li><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><Li>Side slit - 4" in front and 6" in back</li><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/></ul><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/>Ellen shared some finishing techniques:<char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><ul><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><li>To ensure the neck is stretchy enough to go over the head, she worked a loose "around the gatepeg" bind off. </li><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><li>She used the same bind off edges for the top of the sleeves so they wouldn't be too tight in the armhole.<char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><li>To prevent flair at the hem, she cast on with waste yarn and ravel cord. When the knitting was complete, she rehung the cast on edges and bound off tightly not around the gate peg).</li><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><li>After dressing her swatch Ellen discovered that the ribbed stitch pattern she used caused the knitting to relax and become wider and shorter.</li><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><li>With the knit and purl stitch pattern she chose, either side can be the public (right) side</li><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/></ul><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/></string></var><var name='CHALLENGE_ASSIGNID'><string>3389</string></var><var name='CHALLENGE_COMPONENTID'><string>4727</string></var><var name='FIELDNAMES'><string>CHALLENGE_ASSIGNID,CHALLENGE_COMPONENTID,HTMLCONTENT</string></var></struct></data></wddxPacket>

 Have you ever had colors run or fade when you washed your sweater?<br><br><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/>So many knitting disasters can be avoided by swatching and dressing your swatch.  Machine knitters have NO EXCUSE for not swatching!  We can knit multiple swatches quickly, testing stitch patterns and tensions.  Since we don't have a lot of time invested, we can do the "throw-the-swatch-in-the-wash-with-jeans" test to see if a washable yarn will hold up.<BR><BR><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/></string></var></struct></data></wddxPacket>

<wddxPacket version='1.0'><header/><data><struct ><var name='HTMLCONTENT'><string><div class="row"><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><H4>Speak to a group of knitters and they will all have opinions about blocking. For what it's worth, here are my thoughts:</h4><br><br><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><table class="table"><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><tr valign="top"><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><char code='09'/><td><b>Why bother blocking?</b></td><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><char code='09'/><td><em>It adds a professional finish to your knitting.<br>When I was a girl I had a sewing teacher insist that we press every dart and seam as we stitched it. I QUICKLY EMBRACED ... what a difference in the appearance of my finished items! <br><br>Although knitters don't normally press/iron knitting, <b> blocking adds the perfect professional finish.</b></em></td><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/></tr><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><tr valign="top"><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><char code='09'/><td><b>Block the pieces before seaming and finishing?</b></td><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><char code='09'/><td><em>YES!  Why deal with curled edges when you are picking up bands and seaming? A shot of steam goes a long way. (If appropriate for your yarn)</em></td><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/></tr><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><tr valign="top"><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><char code='09'/><td><b>Block the entire garment after it's completed?</b></td><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><char code='09'/><td><em>YES! I like to wash and dry my sweaters before wearing them.<br><br>Many knitters will put their finished sweater in the dryer with a damp towel and let the heat and moisture "block" the finished sweater.</em></td><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/></tr><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><tr valign="top"><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><char code='09'/><td><b>What method to use for blocking?</b></td><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><char code='09'/><td><em><b>OK - this is where you'll find heated discussions.</b><br> <em>When I first started knitting (with acrylic yarn) I was taught to use blocking wires and pin each piece to size on a blocking board. I guess I'm lazy... because I found this to take more time than knitting the whole sweater!</em><br><br><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/>Yes, you need to block ... how you go about it is YOUR CHOICE.<br><br><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/>These days, I use mostly natural fibers and LOVE <b>wet blocking</b>.</em> </td><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/></tr><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/></table><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/></div><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><div class="row"><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><div class="col-md-8 col-xs-12"><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><blockquote class="blockquote_style"><i class="fa fa-quote-left" aria-hidden="true"></i> <b>From long-time MK instructor, Jodie Raymond:</b><br><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><br><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><em><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/> <char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><ul><li><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/>It is wise after finishing  one piece of  your garment,  to block it out to make sure your stitch  gauge is correct.  If this measures correctly, remaining pieces can be knit with confidence.<br><br></li><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><li><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/>Be sure to "tube" (pull) the fabric before blocking.  Also, run a wooden spoon  handle, or dowel,  down through all  doubled pieces like hems, cuffs, bands, and collars before you block in order to set  those stitches.<br><br></li><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><li> Pin out the  fabric on a blocking board and steam until the  piece holds it's shape with no  pins.  This will be the  only time one can  sharply steam the seam  edges - making sewing much easier.  <i class="fa fa-quote-right" aria-hidden="true"></i></li><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/></ul> </em><br><br><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><em><small>Sue's Note: Jodie machine knit in the '80's and specialized in standard gauge dresses, skirts, slacks etc. She use wool/rayon blend, hard-twist dress yarns.<br><br> Adjust your blocking choices based on your style of knitting and yarns used.</em></small><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/></blockquote><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/></div><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><div class="col-md-4 col-xs-12"><img class="img-responsive" src=""><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><i class="fa fa-shopping-cart" aria-hidden="true"></i> Want more information about blocking?<br><a href="/store/product/534/blocking-for-everyone/itemdetails" target="_blank">Printed book available.</a><br><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><br><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><a href="/store/product/534/blocking-for-everyone/itemdetails" target="_blank"><img class="img-responsive" width="200"  src="/knititnow/store/thumbnails/blocking_cover.jpg"></a></div><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/></div><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/></string></var><var name='CHALLENGE_COMPONENTID'><string>2544</string></var><var name='FIELDNAMES'><string>CHALLENGE_ASSIGNID,CHALLENGE_COMPONENTID,HTMLCONTENT</string></var><var name='CHALLENGE_ASSIGNID'><string>918</string></var></struct></data></wddxPacket>

<wddxPacket version='1.0'><header/><data><struct ><var name='HTMLCONTENT'><string><div class="row cleanwell"><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><div class="col-md-7"><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><h4><strong>GAUGE SWATCH</strong></h4><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/>The <strong>gauge swatch</strong> is the "official" swatch used when designing a garment.<char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><br><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/>It is knit at a specific size, marked for accurate stitch and row measurement and "dressed" as the final garment will be treated.<br><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><blockquote class="smallblock"><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><em>TIP: Whatever method you use to create a swatch, the key is to correctly measure it and calculate your gauge.</em></blockquote></div><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><div class="col-md-5"><img class="img-responsive" src="//www.knititnow.com/challenge/images/swatch_measure.jpg" /></div><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/></div></string></var><var name='FIELDNAMES'><string>CHALLENGE_ASSIGNID,TYPEOF,HTMLCONTENT</string></var><var name='CHALLENGE_ASSIGNID'><string>304</string></var><var name='TYPEOF'><string>HTML</string></var></struct></data></wddxPacket>

<wddxPacket version='1.0'><header/><data><struct ><var name='FIELDNAMES'><string>CHALLENGE_ASSIGNID,TYPEOF,HTMLCONTENT</string></var><var name='CHALLENGE_ASSIGNID'><string>304</string></var><var name='HTMLCONTENT'><string><div class="row cleanwell"><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><div class="col-md-12 col-xs-12"><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><h4><strong>TENSION SWATCH</strong></h4><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><em>When I pick up a new cone of yarn, I can't wait to thread up my machine and see what the yarn looks like.   From the initial cast on, I start guessing what setting on my tension dial I need to use.  I knit a few inches and reach down and start to feel the resulting fabric. <br /><br />Once I get a feel for the yarn (what machine, general tension setting at stockinette, etc) I create a<strong> tension swatch</strong>.  This helps me fine-tune the tension needed to achieve the fabric I like and allows me to play with various techniques.  <strong>I'm often very surprised that a yarn looks great in tuck, and awful in slip</strong>, for example.  Adding a few eyelets here and there tells me if the yarn will work up in lace.</em><br /> <br /> Let's practice knitting a <strong>tension swatch.</strong></div><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/></div></string></var><var name='TYPEOF'><string>HTML</string></var></struct></data></wddxPacket>

Knit a marker row (change colors, work a few eyelets across the row or knit a sewing thread in with the main yarn)</li><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><li>Keep knitting sections, marking the tension dial number in each section.  Knit the last section as loosely as possiblle, even if you think this will be too loose ... I'm often very pleasantly surprised at the result.</li><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><li>Transfer every other needle to out of work postion and knit a section - put all needles back into work.</li><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><li>Work a simple tuck, or slip, or any stitch pattern of your choice ... base your tension dial setting on the stockinette sections you just knit.</li><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/></ol><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><blockquote class="smallblock">The point of this exercise is to put the yarn through it's paces ... ignite your creativity, and get a feel for what the yarn can do.  If you don't have a huge cone, you can always re-wind this knitting. Hand knit each stitch to ensure  the tucks knit properly.  After manually knitting one row, Cancel hold on the carriage,  pull the needles all the way out and carefully knit the next row.</li><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/></ul><br><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><i class="fa fa-check-square fa-2x" style="color:#9E2065" aria-hidden="true"></i> <char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><b>Tuck stitch patterns are wider than stockinette.</b> <br> They allow you to knit wider pieces, minimizing the needlebed size limitations (total number of needles available).<br><br><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><i class="fa fa-check-square fa-2x" style="color:#9E2065" aria-hidden="true"></i> <char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><b>Tuck stitch patterns are shorter than stockinette.</b><br> You'll need to knit more rows for the same length.<br><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><br><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><i class="fa fa-check-square fa-2x" style="color:#9E2065" aria-hidden="true"></i> <char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><b>Tuck stitch takes more yarn than other stitch patterns</b><br>Plan accordingly<char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><br><br><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><i class="fa fa-check-square fa-2x" style="color:#9E2065" aria-hidden="true"></i> <char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><b>When manually tucking on your machine, avoid the end needles.</b><br>  Do not tuck the end 1-2 needles for easier seaming and a neater edge.<char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/></div></div></string></var><var name='CHALLENGE_COMPONENTID'><string>4004</string></var><var name='CHALLENGE_ASSIGNID'><string>3117</string></var></struct></data></wddxPacket>

<wddxPacket version='1.0'><header/><data><struct ><var name='HTMLCONTENT'><string>If you haven't yet touched (or attached) your ribber ... <b>hold your horses! </b> <i class="fa fa-smile-o aria-hidden="true"></i><br><br><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/>If you've been able to follow the instructions, cast on and confirm that the ribber is set up correctly and working, you should be good.  We aren't going to create a wardrobe in ribbing (yet <i class="fa fa-smile-o aria-hidden="true"></i><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/>) but <b>the goal is to just take some concentrated time to play and gain confidence.</b><br><br><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/>With that being said, I normally tell newer knitters to master the single bed first.  Learn a couple of cast on methods, be comfortable with stitch patterning ... learn shaping techniques ... learn about what yarns you  like and work best with your machine ... make a few things before attempting the ribber.  With the ribber there are so many more things going on than with just the single bed. <br><br><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/>It's like learning to play the piano.  Start with your dominant hand and pick out a few notes.  Learn the layout of the keys.  Learn to read the music. Practice reading the music and playing without looking .... then add the other hand ....   at some point your feet get in the act. (OK - you can tell that I don't teach piano, but you get the idea) <br><br><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><b>With a double bed setup, you need to keep track of 2 machines and UNDERSTAND what's going on with BOTH of them (at the same time).</b><br><br><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/>If you feel you aren't for the Knit-along right now, you might want to take time to watch the videos and start getting a picture of what the ribber is all about. <b> It's not hard!</b>  But we don't want to cause any tears because you aren't ready.<br><br><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/>Although participating "live" gives you access to the forum and hopefully encourages you to MAKE TIME to knit, <b>the content will be available in the Learning Library for you to follow later (when you are ready)</b><br><br><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><b>PS</b><br><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><em>If this initial Knit-along seems to basic for you ... we have more scheduled. (and we couldn't start with double bed jacquard in good conscience <i class="fa fa-smile-o aria-hidden="true"></i>)</em> Stay tuned!</string></var><var name='CHALLENGE_ASSIGNID'><string>3209</string></var><var name='FIELDNAMES'><string>CHALLENGE_ASSIGNID,CHALLENGE_COMPONENTID,HTMLCONTENT</string></var><var name='CHALLENGE_COMPONENTID'><string>4260</string></var></struct></data></wddxPacket>

<wddxPacket version='1.0'><header/><data><struct ><var name='HTMLCONTENT'><string>we've spent a lot of time planning, practicing and thinking about knitting ... are you ready to do some "real knitting"?<br><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><br><strong>DON'T SKIP THIS SECTION!</strong> <br><br>Your success with this course AND your success with your knitting machine depends on your understanding and mastering the art of knitting gauge swatches.<br><br><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/>Without a swatch we are knitting in the dark.<char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><ul><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><li>How is the final sweater going to feel in the yarn and stitch pattern you've chosen?</li><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><li>Do you have enough yarn?</li><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><li>Do you have enough needles on your machine for the size you chose?</li><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/></ul><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><div class="row"><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><div class="col-md-6 col-lg-5 col-xs-12 col-md-offset-1 text-center"><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><p style="text-align: center;"><strong>SWATCHING IS NOT OPTIONAL</strong></p><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><img class="img-thumbnail" src="//www.knititnow.com/images/blog_images/2017/swatching_is_not_optional.jpg" /></div><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/></div></string></var><var name='CHALLENGE_ASSIGNID'><string>3346</string></var><var name='CHALLENGE_COMPONENTID'><string>4634</string></var><var name='FIELDNAMES'><string>CHALLENGE_ASSIGNID,CHALLENGE_COMPONENTID,HTMLCONTENT</string></var></struct></data></wddxPacket>

<wddxPacket version='1.0'><header/><data><struct ><var name='HTMLCONTENT'><string><div class="row"><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><div class="col-md-6 col-xs-12"><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/>Measuring a swatch flat isn't always the best way to measure gauge.  Your knitting is going to be hanging on your body. Consider the weight of the entire piece of knitting. If you are a hand knitter, think of it this way, a larger needle will produce a large stitch, and therefore a more open knitted fabric. Also the weight of the yarn impacts the size of the stitch and the finished appearance of the knitted fabric.<br><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><br><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/>With the LK-150 you can use a fine yarn- think of a sock weight yarn. or a #1.  Because of the size of the hooks, the distance between the hooks and the setting of the tension dial, you can create very different fabrics  even in plain stockinette knitting.<br><br><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/>At the opposite end of the spectrum you can use a  medium #4 weight yarn and create a hand knit look.<br><br><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/>For heavier yarns, you even have the option of knitting over every other needle.<char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><br><br><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/>Something to consider ... the size of the hook of the needle determines the thickest yarn you can use.  If you try to use a very bulky (or maybe a hand spun yarn) and it doesn't fit in the hooks of the needles, you'll be splitting the yarn and the stitches won't form properly.<br><br><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><blockquote class="blockquote_style"><i class="fa fa-lightbulb-o fa-2x aria-hidden="true"></i><br><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><ul class="lightlist" style="list-style:none;"><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><li>Think of the <b>Carriage Stitch/Tension Dial</b> as the hand knitting needle size.<br><br></li><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><li>Think of the <b>Mast Tension Dial</b> as the tension a hand knitter would apply to the yarn with her fingers</li><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/></blockquote><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/></div><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><div class="col-sm-3 col-xs-12"><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><char code='09'/><figure><img class="img-thumbnail" src="/challenge/images/v2/50/Tension_mast_dial.jpg"><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><figcaption align="center"><br><b>Tension Dial</b></figcaption><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/></figure><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/></div><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/></div><br><br><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/></string></var><var name='FIELDNAMES'><string>CHALLENGE_ASSIGNID,CHALLENGE_COMPONENTID,HTMLCONTENT</string></var></struct></data></wddxPacket>

<wddxPacket version='1.0'><header/><data><struct ><var name='CHALLENGE_COMPONENTID'><string>156</string></var><var name='FIELDNAMES'><string>CHALLENGE_ASSIGNID,CHALLENGE_COMPONENTID,HTMLCONTENT</string></var><var name='HTMLCONTENT'><string><div class="row cleanwell"><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><div class="col-md-7"><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><h4><strong>GAUGE SWATCH</strong></h4><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/>The <strong>gauge swatch</strong> is the "official" swatch used when designing a garment.<char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><br><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/>It is knit at a specific size, marked for accurate stitch and row measurement and "dressed" as the final garment will be treated.<br><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><blockquote class="smallblock"><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><em>TIP: Whatever method you use to create a swatch, the key is to correctly measure it and calculate your gauge.</em></blockquote></div><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><div class="col-md-5"><img class="img-responsive" src="//www.knititnow.com/challenge/images/swatch_measure.jpg" /></div><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/></div></string></var><var name='CHALLENGE_ASSIGNID'><string>58</string></var></struct></data></wddxPacket>

<wddxPacket version='1.0'><header/><data><struct ><var name='CHALLENGE_ASSIGNID'><string>58</string></var><var name='HTMLCONTENT'><string><div class="row cleanwell"><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><div class="col-md-12 col-xs-12"><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><h4><strong>TENSION SWATCH</strong></h4><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><em>When I pick up a new cone of yarn, I can't wait to thread up my machine and see what the yarn looks like.   From the initial cast on, I start guessing what setting on my tension dial I need to use.  I knit a few inches and reach down and start to feel the resulting fabric. <br /><br />Once I get a feel for the yarn (what machine, general tension setting at stockinette, etc) I create a<strong> tension swatch</strong>.  This helps me fine-tune the tension needed to achieve the fabric I like and allows me to play with various techniques.  <strong>I'm often very surprised that a yarn looks great in tuck, and awful in slip</strong>, for example.  Adding a few eyelets here and there tells me if the yarn will work up in lace.</em><br /> <br /> Let's practice knitting a <strong>tension swatch.</strong></div><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/></div></string></var><var name='FIELDNAMES'><string>CHALLENGE_ASSIGNID,CHALLENGE_COMPONENTID,HTMLCONTENT</string></var><var name='CHALLENGE_COMPONENTID'><string>258</string></var></struct></data></wddxPacket>

<wddxPacket version='1.0'><header/><data><struct ><var name='FIELDNAMES'><string>CHALLENGE_ASSIGNID,CHALLENGE_COMPONENTID,HTMLCONTENT</string></var><var name='CHALLENGE_COMPONENTID'><string>4490</string></var><var name='CHALLENGE_ASSIGNID'><string>3308</string></var><var name='HTMLCONTENT'><string><div class="row well"><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><div class="col-xs-12 col-md-10"><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><h4>Play!</h4><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><ol class="instruction-list"><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><li>Start knitting stockenette at the tightest tension that will knit.  (If the tension is too tight, you'll see stitches that don't form properly.</li><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><li>Knit 2-4 inches. Knit a marker row (change colors, work a few eyelets across the row or knit a sewing thread in with the main yarn)</li><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><li>Keep knitting sections, marking the tension dial number in each section.  Knit the last section as loosely as possiblle, even if you think this will be too loose ... I'm often very pleasantly surprised at the result.</li><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><li>Transfer every other needle to out of work postion and knit a section - put all needles back into work.</li><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><li>Work a simple tuck, or slip, or any stitch pattern of your choice ... base your tension dial setting on the stockinette sections you just knit.</li><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/></ol><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><blockquote class="smallblock">The point of this exercise is to put the yarn through it's paces ... ignite your creativity, and get a feel for what the yarn can do.  If you don't have a huge cone, you can always re-wind this knitting. <wddxPacket version='1.0'><header/><data><struct ><var name='CHALLENGE_ASSIGNID'><string>3473</string></var><var name='FIELDNAMES'><string>CHALLENGE_ASSIGNID,CHALLENGE_COMPONENTID,HTMLCONTENT</string></var><var name='CHALLENGE_COMPONENTID'><string>4891</string></var><var name='HTMLCONTENT'><string><div class="row"><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><div class="col-sm-6 col-xs-12"><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><h3>Knitting a “Proper” Swatch</h3><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/>The goal of a swatch is to determine how many stitches and rows it takes to knit a 1” (or 4”/10cm) square.<br><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/>To do this accurately, you will knit a larger piece, and mark of a set number of stitches and rows AS YOU KNIT.<br><br><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/>After you dress (rest, wash, block) your swatch, you can easily measure and calculate your stitch and row gauge.<char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><br><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/>When you knit your swatch, you will cast on MORE stitches and knit MORE rows than shown. BlockTitle: Knit 'n Purl Stitches on the Machine
details: <wddxPacket version='1.0'><header/><data><struct ><var name='CHALLENGE_ASSIGNID'><string>3503</string></var><var name='HTMLCONTENT'><string><div class="row"><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><div class="col-sm-6 col-xs-12"><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/>One of the first surprises for most machine knitters is the fact that the humble garter stitch is problematic on the knitting machine. Because our needles face in one direction and they form uniform stitches in one direction, we can easily produce stockinette stitch (translated knit 1 row, purl 1 row) but to knit every row?…..<br><br><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/>Be default, knitting machines knit stockinette stitch. Stockinette has a smooth side (knit) side and a bumpy side (purl side)<char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/>In hand knitting terms this is knit 1 row purl 1 row.<char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/>Hand knitters can easily knit garter stitch by knitting every row. <wddxPacket version='1.0'><header/><data><struct ><var name='HTMLCONTENT'><string>Because the needles on our needlebeds are positioned in one direction, passing the carriage and knitting a row produces stitches with the purl bumps facing.<br><br><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/>You might want purl bumps on the opposite side of the knitting:<char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><ul><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><li>Ribbing</li><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><li>Garter stitch accent rows</li><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><li>Vertical accents between cables</li><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><li>Accents to eyelets for lace</li><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/></ul><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><b>To reform individual Stitches:</b><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><ol><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><li>Use your latch tool to remove an individual stitch from the machine needle</li><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><li>Insert the hook of the latch tool in the stitch in the row below</li><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><li>Release the loose stitch</li><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><li>Place the stitch behind the latch</li><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><li>Place the unknit strand in the hook of the tool</li><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><li>Pull the strand through, closing the latch with the stitch and forming a new stitch</li><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><li><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/>Replace the new stitch back on the machine</li><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><li>Notice that the purl bump is now away from you</li><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/></ul><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/></string></var><var name='CHALLENGE_ASSIGNID'><string>3521</string></var><var name='FIELDNAMES'><string>CHALLENGE_ASSIGNID,CHALLENGE_COMPONENTID,HTMLCONTENT</string></var><var name='CHALLENGE_COMPONENTID'><string>5015</string></var></struct></data></wddxPacket>

What happens?</li><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><li>With the RIGHT Russel Lever set to plain knitting, pass the carriage.  What happens?</li><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><li>Put a few needles in hold</Li><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><li>Engage both Russel Levers (set your carriage to hold in both directions)</li><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><li>Pass the carriage back and forth. This means it takes 2 passes of the carriage to complete each NECKLINE INCREASE SEQUENCE.<br>(The purpose of this is to increase neatly with automatic wraps and prevent holes between the neckline edge and the neckband)</li><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/>        </ul><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/>        These increase are worked AT THE SAME TIME<br><br><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/>    </div><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/>        <div class="col-sm-6 col-xs-12"><img class="img-responsive" src="/challenge/images/v2/55/neck_shaping.jpg"><br></div><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/></div><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/>       <div class="row"><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><div class="col-sm-10 col-sm-offset-1 col-xs-12"><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/>        <char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/>        <div style="color:green;"><b>Neckline Increase Sequence (left side of needlebed): </b><br><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/>            <ol class="li_7px"><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/>                <li>Carriage set to hold</li><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/>                <li>Carriage on the LEFT</li><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/>                <li>On the carriage side: Put 2 needles with stitches into working position<br>~and~ put ONE EMPTY NEEDLE into working position<br><em>This increases 1 raglan stitch on the left and 1 neckline stitch (plus a stitch for wrapping) on the right</em></li><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/>                <li>Knit to the RIGHT</li><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/>                <li>On the carriage side (right): Pull 1 needle to hold position for automatic wrap<br><em>This prevents a hole</em></li><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/>                <li>Knit to the LEFT <em>(2 needles in work)</em></li><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/>            </ol><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/>            This completes the NECKLINE INCREASE SEQUENCE for the left side. If you struggle, try a stitch pattern with needles that are knitting next to the needles out of work. (For Brother machines try using KCII)</li><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><li>Don't forget tuck brushes!</li><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><li>Plan for the position of the needles out of work... you don't want them right at the edge of your knitting</li><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><li>Don't let your machine tuck the edge stitches. Learn about end needle selection on your machine</li><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/></ol><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><b>The Challenge:</b><br><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><ol><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><li>Choose a tuck lace pattern from the punchcards or stitch patterns that came with your machine. When the lace carriage is passed in one direction stitches on selected needles are picked up, removed and transferred to an adjoining needle. But what if you want to position your eyelet away from the transferred stitch?<br><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><center><img class="image-thumbnail" src="https://www.knititnow.com/challenge/images/v2/58/multi_transfer1.jpg"></center><br><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/>It would take multiple passes of the lace carriage to create this.<br><br><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/>In order to make multiple passes and move stitches without knitting them you need to:<char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><ul><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><li>Remove the yarn from the yarn feeder AND</li><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><li>Set the carriage to knit Fashion Lace</li><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/></ul><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/>As always, it's critical to have your manual and understand the settings for your machine.<br><br><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><a data-vimeoid="369332867" class="videopopup"><i class="fa fa-youtube-play" aria-hidden="true"></i>  More on multiple stitch transfers and Fashion Lace</a><br><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><br><em>NOTE: Studio/Silver/Singer Fashion Lace punchcards have red indicators on the rows to pass the carriage without yarn AND change the carriage setting.  BUT, any lace punchcard that has multiple stitch transfers can be used. The key is understanding how these cards are punched and understanding the function of the lace carriage.</em><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/></div><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><div class="col-sm-4 col-xs-12"><figure><img class="img-responsive" src="/challenge/images/v2/58/studioL10.jpg"><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><figcaption align="center"><br>Singer Fashion Lace punchcard</figcaption><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/></figure><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/></div><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/></div></string></var></struct></data></wddxPacket>

(DUH)<char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/>On my standard machine, I've dutifully cast on 60 stitches and knit 60 rows between marked rows .  I marked off 40 stitches and got out my regular ruler, measured and did the math.<char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><em>Being a total non-math person, I can't tell you how many times I've messed up the calculation of my gauge ... even when using a calculator.</em><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><br><br><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/> <char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><div class="row"><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><div class="col-md-2 col-xs-12" align="center"><img class="img-responsive" src="http://kin.knititnow.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/05/lightbulb_guy_100.jpg" alt="" width="50" /></div><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><div class="col-md-10 col-xs-12"><img class="img-responsive" src=""><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><br><br><br><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><strong>THE EPIPHANY:</strong> I was hand knitting a HK pattern.  Hand knitting the complicated sections of the pattern was fun, but I decided that knitting a whole lot of stockinette (the boring stuff by hand) was dumb.  So I threaded up my machine and started to knit a swatch.<char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/></div><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/></div><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><br><br><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><b>The gauge I needed to match was 24 sts and 30 rows per 4".</b><br><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><ul class="li_7px"><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/> <char code='09'/><li> I cast 60 stitches (so I could easily measure 24 stitches)</li><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/> <char code='09'/><li> I knit a few rows with my main yarn (marking with eyelets the tension gauge)</li><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/> <char code='09'/><li> 2 rows of a contrasting color</li><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/> <char code='09'/><li> Knit 30 rows</li><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/> <char code='09'/><li> 2 rows of a contrasting color</li><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/> <char code='09'/><li> A few main yarn rows and bound off</li><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/> <char code='09'/><li>AT THE SAME TIME I also marked  the stitches that were framing my desired 24 stitches.</li><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/></ul><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><blockquote class="blockquote_style"><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><strong>In other words, instead of marking the traditional number of stitches and rows, I broke the "rules" and marked my DESIRED GAUGE  of 24 stitches and 30 rows as I knit the swatch.</strong></blockquote><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/>I let the swatch rest, then wet blocked it and let it sit overnight.<char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/>The next day, I put my handy-dandy 4" measuring tool down on my swatch.  (see below about my DIY 4" tool)<char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/>As you can see, by the first photo, my stitch gauge was good, but my row gauge needed to be adjusted.  It was easy to see through my tool that I had too many rows to 4".   I adjusted my mast tension, knit another swatch and VOILA!  I was able to match my gauge EXACTLY --- with NO MATH!<br><br><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/> <div class="row"><char code='0d'/><char Gauge is close - but the row gauge is off</strong></div><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><div class="col-12-xs col-md-6"><img src="http:/knititnow.com/challenge/images/v2/25/swatch_compare2-1-300x288.jpg" alt="" width="300" height="288" /><br> <strong>24 sts x 30 rows = 4" ! Success!</strong></div><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/></div><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><hr class="styel13"><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/> <char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><h3>Template</h3><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><div align="center"><img class="img-responsive" src="http://kin.knititnow.com/challenge/images/v2/25/swatch_template.png" alt="" width="342" height="342" /></div><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/>For my tool, I cut a 4" x 4" square of quilters template plastic (readily available at craft stores) to create my Handy-dandy tool. Because it's see-through, I can see my marked stitches and rows on my swatch.<br><br><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/>You could use a square of any material (cardboard, paper, clear plastic of any kind).<br><br><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/>We've created a to-scale template for you to print. Print the template on paper, a transparency or card stock and try it.  You will be amazed at how much easier it is to measure gauge (for both hand and machine knitting).<char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/></string></var><var name='CHALLENGE_COMPONENTID'><string>6291</string></var><var name='FIELDNAMES'><string>CHALLENGE_ASSIGNID,CHALLENGE_COMPONENTID,HTMLCONTENT</string></var></struct></data></wddxPacket>

This will prevent you from measuring edge to edge and ONLY MEASURE the ISOLATED AREA.<br><br><br><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><ol class="instruction-list"><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><li>Garment yarn: Cast on 50 stitches with any method</li><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><li> Knit for 1” or so - carriage on the right</li><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><li>Contrasting waste yarn: Knit 2 rows</li><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><li> Garment yarn: knit 20 rows</li><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><li>Use a yarn marker or run a strand as you knit, isolate the stitches.</li><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><li> Knit 20 rows</li><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><li>Contrasting waste yarn: Knit 2 rows</li><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><li>Garment yarn: knit 1” or so</li><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><li> Bind off or drop the work from the machine</li><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><li> Dress the swatch (wash, block and treat as you will the finished item)</li><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/></ol><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/></div><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><div class="col-sm-4 col-xs-12"><img class="img-responsive" src="/challenge/images/v2/50/lk-150_swatch2.png"></div><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/></div><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/></string></var></struct></data></wddxPacket>
